strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: comprehensive report generation from high-dimensional 3D chest CT, where retaining both global context and localized findings is clinically relevant.

The proposed pipeline is intuitively motivated. R2 pooling combines coverage of all slices with higher-resolution tokens from region-representative slices, while segmentation tokens and structured attributes provide complementary localization cues.

The component ablations show a coherent pattern: region-centric sampling improves the reported clinical metrics over uniform LITA sampling, and combining mask and attribute inputs gives the strongest CA-F1 and GPT-based scores.

Evaluation includes lexical metrics and clinically oriented metrics rather than relying only on BLEU/ROUGE. The manuscript is generally readable, and the architecture and report-generation workflow are illustrated clearly.
The supplementary material provides useful training details, including the backbone, LLM, LoRA configuration, optimization settings, hardware, input resolution, and number of visual tokens.
weaknesses: The evidence does not substantiate the broad state-of-the-art claim. The method is best on only three of six reported metrics; M3D is better on ROUGE-L and METEOR, while CT2Rep is substantially better on GREEN. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, statistical tests, or per-abnormality results are provided, so the significance and consistency of the relatively small gains cannot be assessed.

The baseline protocol is potentially unfair and difficult to interpret. Architectures are retrained or modified to use LLaMA3-8B and constrained to 48 hours on two A100 GPUs; models without suitable pretrained weights are trained from scratch and explicitly described as insufficiently trained. This measures performance under an arbitrary compute constraint rather than providing faithful or compute-matched comparisons to the original methods.

The strongest inputs may expose the answer almost directly. Lesion-specific masks for nodules, cysts, and effusions are converted into counts, diameters, and locations and supplied as text. The paper does not report SAT's test-set segmentation quality, explain how lesion prompts are selected without prior knowledge, or compare predicted masks with oracle, corrupted, and absent masks. Consequently, it is unclear whether the gains come from report generation or from an unmeasured upstream lesion detector, and robustness to segmentation failures is unknown.

The patient-attribute computation appears technically incorrect for physical measurements. The supplementary pseudocode calls voxel counts 'ml' without multiplying by voxel spacing and computes diameter as the maximum axis-aligned bounding-box extent without accounting for spacing, resampling, or Euclidean lesion diameter. Since volumes are resized to 256x256x32, these quantities cannot generally represent valid milliliters or millimeters as the prompt claims.

The claimed efficiency advantage is not evaluated. There are no measurements of FLOPs, memory, throughput, training/inference time, or comparisons at matched token budgets. The method also requires an external 3D segmentation model, whose substantial cost is omitted from the efficiency discussion.

Clinical evidence is inadequate for claims such as reliability, diagnostic fidelity, interpretability, and real-world applicability. Evaluation uses one dataset derived from a single underlying cohort, automated metrics including an incompletely specified GPT-4o-mini judge, and only one cherry-pickable qualitative case. There is no radiologist assessment, external validation, subgroup analysis, or clinically meaningful error analysis.

Originality is limited because the principal pieces are adaptations or combinations of prior work: slow/fast token sampling from LITA, the mask-aware extractor from MAIRA-SEG/Osprey, SAT pseudo-masks, and deterministic mask-to-text attributes motivated by prior visual translators. Region-centric slice selection is sensible but comparatively incremental.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplement: the report-splitting/merging procedure, exact masks and region mappings, prompts, decoding settings, validation protocol, metric implementations and judge prompt, segmentation-token construction, and several pooling parameters are unspecified. The abstract also says the code is public, but the manuscript provides no accessible repository reference.

The manuscript does not meaningfully discuss failure modes or safety limitations, particularly propagation of segmentation errors, hallucinated normal/abnormal findings, scanner/domain shift, and the risks of presenting approximate geometric quantities as clinical measurements. These omissions are important given the clinical deployment language.

strengths: The region-focused formulation is clinically motivated: scan-wide tokens, organ/lesion-specific features, and structured regional generation address limitations of global-only 3D CT representations.
R2 pooling is a practical way to reuse a pretrained 2D medical encoder while substantially reducing the number of tokens passed to the LLM.
The evaluation uses the large public RadGenome-Chest CT dataset, several relevant baselines, lexical and clinical metrics, and component ablations.
The full model obtains the best reported CA-F1 and GPT-4-based scores, suggesting that region and attribute information can improve clinical-content recovery.
weaknesses: The comparison is not sufficiently controlled. MedRegion-CT receives SAT-derived organ and lesion masks plus explicit textual attributes such as lesion class, count, location, and size, whereas the baselines apparently receive only CT volumes. Consequently, the gains may reflect privileged outputs from a powerful external segmenter rather than the proposed visual representation. The paper provides no equal-information baseline, oracle-versus-predicted-mask comparison, segmentation accuracy, or robustness analysis under mask errors.

The patient-specific measurements are technically problematic. The supplementary pseudocode calls voxel counts “volume” without applying voxel spacing and estimates lesion “diameter” as the largest axis-aligned bounding-box extent, again without physical spacing. These are not valid clinical volume or diameter measurements, undermining claims about quantitative biomarkers and clinical reliability.

The state-of-the-art claim is overstated. The method wins only three of six metrics, trails M3D on ROUGE-L and METEOR, and trails CT2Rep substantially on GREEN. Its BLEU-4 gain over M3D is only 0.002 and CA-F1 gain is 0.015, with no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

Baseline fairness is further weakened by imposing a fixed 48-hour, two-GPU training budget and acknowledging that CT2Rep was insufficiently trained. Architectures with different convergence behavior cannot be reliably ranked under this setup, and comparison against published or fully converged results is absent.

Evidence for clinical usefulness is inadequate. There is no radiologist evaluation, finding-level sensitivity/specificity analysis, rare-abnormality breakdown, external validation, or study of clinically consequential hallucinations. The qualitative assessment contains only one selected COVID-19 case.

The ablations do not fully disentangle structured report splitting, R2 sampling, segmentation tokens, and textual lesion attributes. In particular, directly verbalizing lesion-mask outputs can nearly solve portions of the target report and may introduce label-like shortcuts.

Computational efficiency is a central motivation, yet the paper reports no memory, throughput, latency, FLOPs, or accuracy-efficiency comparison. The claimed benefit of reducing tokens therefore remains unverified at the system level.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: region-merging and report-splitting procedures are underspecified; the exact SAT prompts/checkpoints and handling of absent or failed masks are unclear; and GPT-4o-mini evaluation lacks version, prompt, decoding settings, and reliability analysis. The manuscript asserts public code but provides no identifiable repository link.

The paper makes strong claims of interpretability, real-world applicability, and reliable reporting without directly evaluating interpretability or discussing deployment risks from segmentation failure, measurement errors, and automated clinical report generation. Overall, the idea has merit, but these concerns leave the central scientific and clinical claims insufficiently supported.

strengths: The manuscript presents a coherent Algorithms/General contribution: a practical 3D CT-reporting framework combining region-aware token pooling, segmentation-derived representations, and structured patient attributes. The clinical motivation and overall architecture are clearly explained. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/a729893c40ae448ba1b27b7dd4db46ae/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

R2 Token Pooling is a sensible and computationally attractive adaptation of slow-fast representations: it preserves coverage of every slice while allocating higher-resolution tokens to representative anatomical slices, reducing the nominal token count from D×T to D+T.
The structured generation of six anatomical sections is well aligned with radiological reporting practice and offers a plausible route to more complete and interpretable reports.

The evaluation covers complementary lexical and clinical metrics. On RadGenome-Chest CT, the full method improves over the evaluated baselines in BLEU-4, CA-F1, and GPT-based assessment; the CA-F1 gain over M3D (0.450 versus 0.435) is particularly relevant to the paper's clinical-accuracy objective.

The component studies provide useful evidence: R2 improves all reported LM-based metrics over uniform LITA sampling, while mask and attribute information substantially improve CA-F1 and GPT-based scores over R2 alone. Implementation details in the supplement are reasonably extensive.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is limited to one dataset derived from CT-RATE, without external-institution testing, expert radiologist assessment, statistical uncertainty, or subgroup analysis. This does not adequately support claims of real-world clinical applicability, consistency, or reliability.

The patient-attribute computation appears technically problematic. The pseudocode reports voxel counts as organ volumes and bounding-box extents as lesion diameters, without applying voxel spacing or describing conversion to mL and mm. Because volumes are resized to 256×256×32, these quantities may not represent physical measurements, despite being presented to the LLM with clinical units.

The system depends heavily on SAT-generated organ and lesion masks, yet mask accuracy, failure propagation, inference cost, and performance with imperfect or missing masks are not evaluated. Consequently, improvements may partly reflect the diagnostic capability already embedded in the segmentation model, and the claimed interpretability is not validated.

The baseline protocol is insufficiently controlled and documented. Replacing each method's decoder with LLaMA3-8B, training some models from scratch, and imposing a uniform 48-hour budget may disadvantage architectures with different optimization requirements. It is also unclear whether baselines receive the same six-region supervision and generation protocol.

Several claims overstate the evidence. The full model does not consistently outperform its ablations: R2+Attr has higher BLEU-4 and GREEN, while R2+Mask has higher METEOR. The full model also trails M3D on ROUGE-L and METEOR and CT2Rep on GREEN. The dismissal of CT2Rep's GREEN result as normal-case overfitting is asserted without supporting analysis.

The novelty is moderate because the principal ingredients closely build on LITA, MAIRA-SEG/Osprey, SAT, and prior deterministic visual-to-text translators. Important details of R2 selection and token alignment remain ambiguous, and no runtime, memory, or token-efficiency measurements substantiate the efficiency claim. The evaluation prompts and settings for GPT-4o Mini—called a 'GPT-4 score'—are also not fully specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision and clinical problem: preserving localized evidence while compressing large 3D CT volumes for report generation.
The proposed system is coherent: region-guided SlowFast tokens, organ-mask tokens, and explicit lesion attributes provide complementary global, regional, and quantitative information.

Evaluation is broader than usual, covering 1,551 internal test scans, 500 external scans, multiple report metrics, component ablations, region-wise analysis, lesion-size analysis, mask perturbations, and a blinded reader study.

The reported internal improvements are substantial, particularly for GREEN (0.4555 versus 0.4013 for the strongest baseline) and GPT-CA (0.4003 versus 0.3733). The method also leads all reported clinical metrics in the external zero-shot evaluation.

Baselines are initialized from official weights and fine-tuned on the same structured training set, making the principal internal comparison more meaningful. Bootstrap confidence intervals are also reported.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the supplementary material provides useful preprocessing, optimization, taxonomy, and attribute-extraction details.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the methodological originality is moderate: the work primarily combines adaptations of SlowFast tokenization, Osprey-style mask pooling, an existing universal segmentor, and textual attribute prompting. It may be stronger as an Applied/Systems contribution, but that framing would require more rigorous validation of the complete pipeline and its operational tradeoffs.

The submission omits the identity and basic characteristics of the external dataset throughout the manuscript. Consequently, its acquisition protocol, population, exclusions, pathology distribution, overlap risk, and licensing cannot be assessed. The promised public-code link is also empty, materially limiting reproducibility.

The benchmark labels are produced by a DSPy/Llama-3.3 pipeline, but there is no quantitative validation by radiologists, error analysis, prompt disclosure, or measurement of agreement with the original reports. Because both training and evaluation references are transformed automatically into the proposed six-section format, unknown pipeline errors and templating effects could materially influence all reported results.

The method depends strongly on upstream pseudo-masks, yet segmentation accuracy is not measured on either institution. The perturbation experiment does not define the distortion process or relate it to realistic segmentation errors. Therefore, it does not establish robustness to the actual domain shift faced by TotalSegmentator.

The lesion extractor retains only the largest connected component within each region and emits explicit absence prompts when segmentation finds nothing. This can discard multiple lesions and propagate false negatives as authoritative text. The limitation is consequential: TotalSegmentator misses 110 of 160 stated micro-nodule cases, and the proposed system's small-nodule detection rate is only 0.1270, far below every baseline (0.2857–0.3651).

The clinical validation is too weak for claims of reliability or clinical utility. Only one senior resident evaluates a nominal 50 cases using an unvalidated single 1–10 score against reference reports; there is no second reader, inter-rater agreement, pathology-specific sensitivity, or paired significance analysis. Moreover, every reported mean is an exact multiple of 1/48, which appears inconsistent with the claimed 50 evaluated cases and requires clarification.

The paper repeatedly characterizes gains as significant, but reports confidence intervals for individual systems rather than paired confidence intervals or hypothesis tests for performance differences. Several component gains are very small with overlapping intervals, especially for the mask extractor.

Important efficiency claims are unsupported: there is no token-count distribution, runtime, memory, parameter count, training cost, or comparison at matched compute. The Slow-path sampling and variable sequence construction are also underspecified, and Equation 3 does not clearly define slice selection or pooling behavior.

The external evaluation still uses only one undisclosed institution and 500 retrospectively sampled cases. This is insufficient to support broad claims of robust cross-institutional generalization, especially given the method's dependence on segmentor behavior and scanner/protocol variation.

The paper does not evaluate clinically important failure modes beyond nodules, such as incorrect laterality, measurement error, multiple lesions, incidental findings outside the fixed taxonomy, or contradictions between visual and attribute tokens. These omissions weaken the claim that the system minimizes hallucinations and provides reliable diagnostic reporting.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision and clinical problem: generating anatomically organized reports from full 3D CT volumes. The region-aware design is well motivated by radiology workflow. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/1bfc27497b6f4d47ae2d6e0fa4107a3a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed system coherently combines region-guided tokenization, organ-mask pooling, and explicit lesion attributes. Although the individual ingredients are largely established, their integration into a 3D CT reporting pipeline is practically interesting.

Experiments cover a sizable internal test set (1,551 scans), a 500-case external set, five baselines, component ablations, bootstrap confidence intervals, region-level results, lesion-size analysis, and a segmentation-noise stress test.

The internal improvements are consistent across all reported metrics; for example, GREEN increases from 0.4013 for the strongest listed baseline to 0.4555. The method also leads the reported LM-based metrics on the external set.

The paper is better characterized as an Applied/Systems contribution than an Algorithms/General contribution: its main value is the clinically motivated assembly of existing segmentation, pooling, prompting, and MLLM techniques. This framing makes the limited algorithmic novelty less problematic, but places greater importance on rigorous system validation.
weaknesses: The central comparison is heavily confounded. MedRegion-CT uses MedSigLIP, explicit TotalSegmentator outputs, and deterministic lesion metadata, whereas the competing models have materially different encoders and pretraining. Fine-tuning all official models on the same reports does not isolate the benefit of the proposed modules. The ablations help only partially and do not include a matched global-token baseline with the same MedSigLIP backbone, token budget, LLM, and training recipe.

The structured benchmark is produced by an Llama-3.3-70B/DSPy pipeline that cleans, filters, and merges the reference reports, but the prompts, validation protocol, failure rate, and radiologist assessment of the transformed labels are absent. Consequently, it is unclear whether the benchmark preserves all findings or introduces systematic artifacts that favor the proposed structured output.

Clinical evidence is inadequate for the strength of the reliability and utility claims. The reader study uses only one senior resident, only 50 stated cases, an unspecified and unvalidated 1–10 score, and no inter-reader agreement or statistical comparison. Moreover, every reported mean is an exact multiple of 1/48, which appears inconsistent with the claimed sample size of 50 and needs explanation.

The method can convert segmentation errors directly into authoritative textual statements such as “No lesion is present.” This is a significant safety risk. The reported small-nodule detection rate is only 0.1270, far below every baseline and the best result of 0.3651, yet there is no uncertainty mechanism, fallback behavior, or systematic false-negative analysis. Calling this merely a lower bound imposed by the segmentor does not resolve the end-to-end system failure.

Several technical details are insufficient or problematic. The SlowFast equations collapse 2D spatial indices into j, use the ambiguous condition m(i,2j), and do not clearly specify sampling, ordering, positional encoding, or token counts. No latency, memory, FLOPs, or sequence-length comparison supports the efficiency claims. The “maximum diameter” is only the largest axis-aligned bounding-box side, and retaining solely the largest connected component discards multifocal lesions.

External validation is difficult to assess because the institution/dataset identity and important cohort details are omitted. There is no demographic or prevalence characterization, scanner/protocol breakdown, temporal split analysis, or evidence that MedSigLIP pretraining does not overlap the evaluation data.

The mask-robustness experiment is underdefined: the exact perturbation process and severity are not reported. It also confirms substantial fragility—distorting organ masks reduces BLEU from 0.3273 to 0.2252—without evaluating realistic TotalSegmentator error distributions or reporting organ/lesion segmentation accuracy on either cohort.

The paper overstates its conclusions. Automatic LM-based metrics, including a GPT-5-nano evaluator whose prompt and configuration are not supplied, are not sufficient to establish minimized hallucination, reliability, or clinical utility. Confidence intervals are reported, but paired significance tests are absent, and at least one ablation interval appears duplicated despite different means.

Reproducibility is currently weak: the abstract's code URL is blank, the report-restructuring prompts and GPT evaluator prompt are missing, baseline adaptation details are sparse, and exact inference and dynamic-token configurations are not given. The paper also lacks a substantive discussion of deployment limitations and harms in this high-stakes setting.

Overall, the system has promising empirical signals, but the confounded comparisons, unvalidated benchmark transformation, segmentation-induced hard false negatives, and weak/internally inconsistent reader study prevent a convincing case for acceptance.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper presents a clinically motivated region-aware framework combining anatomical SlowFast tokenization, mask-pooled regional features, and explicit lesion attributes. The components form a coherent approach to preserving localized evidence in large 3D CT volumes.

The empirical results are strong. On the 1,551-case internal test set, MedRegion-CT leads all five baselines across BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, GREEN, CRG, and GPT-CA. On the 500-case external zero-shot evaluation, it achieves the best three clinical-metric scores while remaining competitive on lexical metrics.

The evaluation is broader than is typical: it includes bootstrap confidence intervals, component and encoder ablations, region-wise results, lesion-size stratification, segmentation-noise stress tests, qualitative examples, and an external radiologist assessment.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, including preprocessing, resolution, windowing, model backbones, LoRA settings, optimization, and training stages. The mask-noise and lesion-size analyses are particularly valuable because they reveal rather than conceal an important failure mode.

The application is significant for computer vision and medical imaging. Structured, region-specific CT reporting is practically relevant, and the reported gains in clinical metrics and external generalization support a positive assessment. weaknesses: The model is strongly dependent on upstream segmentation. For small nodules, its detection rate is only 0.1270, versus 0.3651 for the strongest baseline, and TotalSegmentator misses 110 of 160 micro-nodule cases. This is a consequential limitation for chest CT reporting and makes the paper's broad reliability and hallucination-minimization claims too strong.

Attribution of the gains is not fully convincing. The Mask-Driven Visual Extractor adds only very small improvements over R+Attr, with substantially overlapping confidence intervals. The comparisons also do not fully control for backbone strength, token count, parameter count, or training/inference compute. Sequence-length distributions, memory, throughput, and FLOPs are absent despite efficiency being part of the motivation.

The structured benchmark is produced by an Llama-3.3-70B/DSPy rewriting pipeline, but prompts, complete processing rules, manual quality-control results, and estimates of restructuring errors are not provided. Such transformations can materially affect both supervision and evaluation.

The external dataset is unnamed in the manuscript and lacks demographic, scanner, acquisition, and pathology-distribution details; the rationale for evaluating only 500 of 4,014 available cases is also unclear. Moreover, the asserted public-code link is blank. These omissions limit reproducibility and make the cross-institutional claim harder to interpret.

Clinical validation remains preliminary: the reader study uses only 50 cases and one senior resident, a single subjective 1–10 score, and no inter-reader agreement or comparative significance testing. The proprietary GPT-5-nano evaluation also lacks its prompt, decoding configuration, and repeatability analysis. Several external-result confidence intervals overlap, so claims of superiority would benefit from paired statistical tests.

Some technical details need correction or clarification. Equation 2 selects organ-bearing slices but averages all spatial tokens on those slices, which does not match the claim that features strictly correspond to predefined regions. The construction of the collection of per-organ mask tokens is not fully specified. Retaining only the largest connected lesion component can discard multiple clinically relevant lesions, while a bounding-box extent is a crude proxy for lesion diameter.

The paper lacks a substantive discussion of clinical deployment risks, including missed small lesions, segmentation domain shift, erroneous quantitative prompts, uncertainty communication, and the need for radiologist oversight. A dataset-overlap audit is also needed because MedSigLIP was pretrained on large CT-report corpora that could potentially include evaluation sources.
